1: Every child in the city learns the same bedtime story: a hundred and eight stars fall from heaven, live as heroes, and are called home when they die. Shi Jin never believed it. He believed in his job, his ink, and his morning noodles, until the Commission revised his future between two bites. Now there is a removal squad on the stairs, a stranger with a crossbow on the roof, and no path at all.
2: The trains only stop where the Commission says the city exists. Everywhere else, people like Liu Tang carry what the trains will not: medicine, letters, other people's chances. This morning the system flagged his cargo as contraband and his temper as a crime in progress. Half right, as usual. He is heading for the one man who posts bail for strangers, and the crew is headed the same way.
3: Gongsun Sheng reads weather. Not the sky's, the city's: which street will flood, which crowd will turn, which knock means run. The Commission licenses fortune-telling as entertainment, and entertainment is not allowed to be right. Her last three readings were right. So this morning her stall is a crime scene, her name is a fraud alert, and the rain she predicted is coming down hard on everyone.
4: Lu Junyi built a perfect life: clean record, clean company, a tower with his name in brushed steel. Yesterday a risk consultancy predicted his ruin. Today his own operations chief filed the proof, pre-dated. The Commission froze everything but his hands. A man with nothing left and excellent fencing lessons is waiting in the lobby, and he has decided somebody is going to explain this to him.
5: Below the plates, the city keeps an older city like a secret it is ashamed of. Mu Hong carries the crew through his drowned district, two crates of food on his back, because that is what he does. At the bottom of everything: a dead amusement park on a black lake, lanterns lit, noodles going. A man in a clerk's coat waves them in like he has been expecting them. Everyone here says the same thing. Timely Rain paid.
6: Lin Chong teaches the Commission's enforcers how to hold a spear. Best instructor in the city; his file says so. This morning his file says something new: flagged, predicted homicide, ninety-four percent. He has not raised his voice in ten years. But the Director's son has seen Lin Chong's wife, and wanting her is not a crime the system was built to see. By sundown, the best spear in the city belongs to no one.
7: The story about Lu Zhishen is that he hit an extortionist three times and the man stopped being alive. The story is true. He borrowed a monastery's robes on the way out, and the robes fit, more or less, the way vows do. Tonight a prison transport carries his new friend's teacher through the furnace district, and the Monk is standing in the road, cracking his knuckles at the headlights.
8: Li Kui repossesses things for a living: cars, machines, once an entire carousel. Strongest hands in the undercity, no record of ever using them on a person. Today's work order says: the bail office by the lake, everything inside, the ledger too. Li Kui reads slowly. Then he reads who signed it. Then he brings the work order back to the depot, in pieces, for filing.
9: The bio-farm on the ridge has been closed for years, which is why nobody official saw the tiger. Wu Song was walking home from a wake, three drinks in, when it came through the fence line. The clip runs forty seconds: no weapon, no help, no fear. Eighty million views before the Commission scrubbed it. A tiger that cannot exist, killed by a man who was not scheduled to be brave. Both are now his problem.
10: Hu Sanniang runs the last honest scrapyard on the lake road, which is to say the Commission has scheduled it for demolition twice and twice the paperwork came back bent. Today something big and stone-shouldered walked out of the flooded quarry, and the demolition crews are suddenly nowhere. She was already up on the crane. The crew arrives just in time to watch a woman lasso a monster, and Outer Heaven starts feeling like a place with a future.
11: Wu Yong built prediction models for the Commission until the day she read her own daughter's file. She walked out with two things: the route of the Director's birthday convoy, and a question that will not leave her alone. Why did it let her leave? Downtown, a demoted captain named Yang Zhi is auctioning his family's sword to cover a fine he did not earn. The city is full of people the system is finished with. It adds up to something.
12: Master Zhou taught six hundred students to hold a staff before the Commission decided unlicensed teaching was sedition and made him disappear. Tonight the crew finds the level where the disappeared go: rows of quiet doors, each one a person the city agreed to forget. The Wisdom Star opens doors with paperwork. Black Whirlwind opens them with Black Whirlwind. Between the two methods, everyone walks out.
13: Every year the Director ships himself a birthday present: a convoy of things confiscated from people who loved them. Lineage swords. School scrolls. Somebody's grandmother's spear. This year's route runs through a checkpoint that did not exist last week, staffed by polite strangers offering complimentary drinks to hardworking convoy guards. The Wisdom Star has thought of everything. Except the guard captain with the blue birthmark and the worst luck in the city.
14: The drinks work. The convoy sleeps. The crew lifts a year of stolen inheritances without breaking one bone, which is the plan working exactly. Yang Zhi wakes to an empty road, a career already on fire, and a fresh flag on his file: complicity, predicted, ninety-one percent. He did not take the drink. It did not matter. The system had already written tomorrow, and tomorrow needed a culprit.
15: In the deep market, the crew gives back what the Commission confiscated: a sword to a school that thought its history was ash, a scroll to an old woman who reads it out loud twice. Some of the relics hum when certain hands hold them, and nobody wants to say so first. At the door stands Yang Zhi, jobless, flagged, holding his family sword like a resignation letter. He came to fight somebody. He stays for the noodles.
16: The Commission answers the heist with its favorite hammer: Qin Ming, garrison champion, a man whose temper arrives before his orders do. The Wisdom Star baits him into the flood channels, beats him fair, and sends him home embarrassed. He gets there in time to watch the Commission burn his garrison for the crime of losing. They wrote him off as a failure, so they billed him the fire. He walks back to Outer Heaven carrying the ashes and his mace.
17: Marshal Huyan Zhuo does not lose, and the Commission sends him to prove it. He comes down the lake road with armor columns and a career of medals, and Outer Heaven holds. Beaten fair, he asks for a rematch. Then, on his way out, he passes an enforcement squad burning a food line for the crime of feeding Deviants, and something in the marshal finishes changing sides before the rematch does.
18: The order goes out to every range-master in the city: on sight, Timely Rain, lethal authorization. Hua Rong grew up on that man's bail money. He files his refusal the loud way, from four hundred meters, past three officers' hats and through the warrant sheet pinned to the wall. Nobody is hurt. Everybody is informed. The finest shot in the Commission's ranks would like Outer Heaven to know he is coming, and he brings his own bow.
19: Somebody records Timely Rain, three cups deep, asking the quiet question: if the path is written, who holds the pen? By morning it has trended in every ward at once, for exactly ninety-four seconds, and then it is sedition. The sentence comes down before the arrest does. Death, publicly streamed, as a lesson about gratitude. The crew splits: rescue him, or hide him deeper. Nobody notices yet that the leak came from nowhere at all.
20: Dai Zong once delivered a heart across the city in nineteen minutes, in traffic, on foot. Nobody knows how his legs do it and he has stopped explaining. Today he arrives at Outer Heaven with the execution date, the platform layout, and the guard rotation, all before the Commission announces any of it. He also brings an invoice. One rescue plan, he says, costs one bowl of noodles. Payable in advance.
21: The plaza has one unwatched approach: the old river gate, six hundred meters of black water. The fish market's diving champion, Zhang Shun, agrees to guide them, right after settling a small matter of principle with the loud one who called swimming falling, but slower. Land against water goes the way it always goes. Black Whirlwind learns respect, mostly by swallowing half the canal, and Outer Heaven gains the river.
22: Execution day. The stream opens on schedule, the plaza packed with citizens invited to learn about gratitude. Then the broadcast hiccups: a court order nobody issued, read by a voice from nowhere, granting a stay the system never predicted. In the confusion the rain hits, the river gate opens, and the fastest legs in the city cross the platform. The lesson the crowd learns is not the one that was scheduled. The city cheers like it means it.
23: There is no clean way home from a miracle. The Commission floods every road with everything it owns, and the crew scatters through the wild belt beyond the plates, where a man in a traveler's coat keeps ceremony to a minimum and a pouch of smooth stones does the arguing. Zhang Qing covers the retreat one skipped stone at a time, then strolls into Outer Heaven like he had been headed there anyway.
24: The rescue costs the city's patience. Purge sweeps take the wards one by one, politely, thoroughly, and every family that ever waved at the crew finds its permits under review. Outer Heaven absorbs the refugees and learns to sleep in shifts. On the park's dry wave pool, Timely Rain hangs a lantern for every new name in his ledger. It is starting to look crowded up there. Nobody says the number out loud.
25: The Commission's answer is quiet this time. The crew meets an enforcement squad that moves wrong: their timing, their feints, their favorite tricks, played back at them like a recording. Replicas, trained on footage of every fight the crew ever won. The same week the dock fleets are seized, and the wildest of the fisher brothers sails his boat straight up the under-lake, laughing, with the seizure notice nailed to the mast.
26: They call it the Flawless One, and it is: a synthetic fighter built from everyone's best day. It knows Panther Head's spear, the Pilgrim's hands, the Wanderer's angles. The crew loses ground for the first hour of their lives. Then the Skilled Doctor tells a joke at the worst possible moment, the whole line laughs, timing breaks, and the perfect thing built from their footage meets the one minute nobody ever filmed.
27: The beast wave hits the market at noon, exactly when enforcement rotates out, exactly where the stalls are fullest. No model flags it. The Tigress holds the school gate with a cleaver and a soup pot until every child is through, and does not come through herself. Outer Heaven learns what the park sounds like when the kitchen goes dark. The Monk does not say anything about scoreboards for a long time.
28: Grief wants a target, and the Pilgrim finds one: the depot that stood down while the market burned. What the crew does there is effective, and filmed, and hard to watch. For one night they look exactly like what the bulletins say they are. Dragon in the Clouds stands in the wreckage and says the quiet thing out loud: our luck has a shape. Even the bad kind. Especially the bad kind.
29: Constable Zhu Tong has covered for the undercity his whole career: a warning here, a slow report there, a beard that made even an arrest feel courteous. The precinct finally audits its own kindness and finds him guilty of all of it. They take the badge and leave the beard. He walks his old beat one last time, all the way down the lake road, and knocks on Outer Heaven's gate like a man reporting for duty.
30: The city starts talking back. Thank-you notes on the park fence, soup left at the gate, a mural of a tiger nobody will admit painting. And down from the hills comes a hunter with beast-sign maps a year deep: the monsters are not wandering, they are being herded, driven along survey lines toward wherever Deviants gather. Somebody is aiming the wilderness. Xie Zhen, the Two-Headed Snake, wants to know who, and his sister is already tracking.
31: The mountain has a king: an old horned beast that never once came below the tree line, until a Commission survey barge parked over its den and started pinging. Maddened, it comes down on the crew like weather. Xie Bao, the Twin-Tailed Scorpion, drops out of a pine mid-sentence, finishing one her brother started a week ago, and between the two of them the hunt turns. The beast dies angry. The barge, they notice, was never armed. It was measuring.
32: Past the border weirs, where the Witch keeps an inn the Commission pretends not to see, the crew meets the other story: the Southbank, Old Fang's people, outlaws with no flags in their files because the system cannot read them at all. Rougher. Freer. Unwritten. Two crews, one table, knives politely visible. The Witch feeds both sides and threatens to sell whoever starts something. Nobody starts something. Everyone leaves unsettled.
33: Somebody hits three Southbank family barges in the night, wearing the crew's colors and using the crew's tricks. Somebody hits the Witch's inn the same hour, wearing Southbank knots. By dawn the border is a wound and both sides are certain. The Wisdom Star runs the timings and goes very quiet: two attacks, one author, no flags anywhere. Someone is writing them into a war, and the handwriting is from nowhere.
34: Xu Ning arrives first, a drill instructor with a lineage older than the plates, come to teach the crew how to open Commission armor. The envoy arrives second, gilt-edged and smiling: full amnesty. Names cleared, identities restored, enforcer badges for every hand at Outer Heaven. One condition, said gently, twice: the Southbank ends. The crew looks at the badges, the ledger, and each other. The vote is called for morning.
35: Timely Rain argues yes. The man who never asked anyone for anything asks for this: take the badges, end the running, buy every name in the ledger a legal tomorrow. Black Whirlwind puts his fist through a carousel horse and votes no with the splinters. The yes wins. The badges are handed out in the rain, and every hand that takes one feels the same small wrongness, like a coat cut for somebody else.
36: The Southbank campaign opens exactly as briefed, which should be the first warning. Every bridge falls on schedule. Every ambush is pre-cleared. The crew wins and wins and feels like a hand inside a glove inside a fist. Today's orders: the third bridge. Hold it four minutes so the families can cross. Fiery Thunderbolt volunteers before anyone finishes reading. Bridges, he says, are honest work.
37: Old Fang's dock is the last Southbank hold, and the Commission wants it drowned: flood-charges on the water gate, timed for high tide, families still inside the line. The crew is ordered to secure the gate and watch. Nobody plans to watch. White Streak checks the sluice twice and says nothing, which from him is a speech. The river is calm today. The river is never calm here.
38: The wall of names is longer than the menu now. The Wisdom Star stops sleeping and starts charting: every victory the crew ever won, plotted; every lucky break, dated; every loss, priced. The curve is smooth. Training-smooth. Selection-smooth. And in the founder-era archives, one artifact: a roster, one hundred and eight lines, formatted exactly like a kind man's ledger. The ascension invitation arrives within the hour, gilt-edged, addressed to the survivors by name.
39: Ascension Day. The tower opens like a church. Below the last floor there is no machine, no god, no code: jars. Rows of old minds in warm fluid, watching through the walls, and a recording in the founder's own voice, practicing the star legend until it sounded kind. On a screen a life plays back: a clerk who always had bail money, built kindness by kindness to gather the best. Timely Rain watches his whole self turn into handwriting.
40: The council does not rage. It schedules. Guardians unfold from the tower's bones, harvest machinery warms up two floors down, and the exits reprice themselves by the second. The crew carries the truth toward daylight through everything the Commission owns. Someone has to hold the stairwell. Someone has to hold the yard. Nobody says it out loud. The rearguard sorts itself the way it always has, oldest soldiers first.
41: There is one way to starve a harvest: leave it nothing ripe. The survivors choose it together, out loud, once, and nobody argues, which is how you know it is real. First the engine two floors under the tower dies, so the taken minds go free. Then the park, the wave pool, one cup passed around like the end of any good dinner. The Commission's models scream at a plan with no pattern and no price. The crew walks in calm.
42: Years now. A new district, new lights, a clerk losing his job to a prediction he does not understand. On the stairwell home, a kid is telling her little brother the old story: the park, the lanterns, the last stand nobody filmed. Every kid tells it a little differently. This is how she tells it. This is the part where the hundred and eight stood up.
